title: Cranial Nerves Beyond the Brainstem
summary: The peripheral journeys of the cranial nerves through skull, face and neck, plus the autonomic wiring of the head.

lessons.title: Trigeminal Divisions V1, V2 & V3: Peripheral Course and Territories

levels.kid:
Your face has a giant helper nerve called the **trigeminal nerve**. "Tri" means three, because it splits into three big branches, like a tree trunk splitting into three limbs.

- The top branch feels your forehead and eyes.
- The middle branch feels your cheeks, nose and top teeth.
- The bottom branch feels your chin and bottom teeth. It also moves your chewing muscles!

When a fly lands on your cheek, this nerve sends a message to your brain: "Something is touching me!" When you crunch an apple, the bottom branch tells your jaw muscles to squeeze.

Dentists use this nerve too. When they numb your bottom teeth, they put medicine near the bottom branch so you feel no pain.
levels.hs:
The **trigeminal nerve** is cranial nerve V (CN V), the main **sensory** nerve of the face. It is the largest cranial nerve. Its sensory cell bodies sit in the **trigeminal ganglion**, a lump inside the skull. From there it splits into three **divisions**:

- **V1, ophthalmic**: forehead, upper eyelid, the eye's surface (cornea), and the top and tip of the nose. It is purely sensory.
- **V2, maxillary**: lower eyelid, cheek, side of the nose, upper lip and upper teeth. It is purely sensory.
- **V3, mandibular**: lower lip, chin, lower teeth, part of the tongue's feeling, and skin in front of the ear. It is the only division that is **mixed**: it also carries **motor** fibers to the **muscles of mastication** (chewing), such as the masseter and temporalis.

Each division leaves the skull through its own hole, or **foramen**: V1 through the superior orbital fissure, V2 through the foramen rotundum, and V3 through the foramen ovale ("Standing Room Only").

A real example: **shingles** of the V1 area (herpes zoster ophthalmicus). The virus hides in the trigeminal ganglion and later reactivates as a painful rash along V1. A rash on the tip of the nose, called **Hutchinson's sign**, warns that the eye itself may be involved. That is because the nose tip and the eye share a branch, the nasociliary nerve.
levels.college:
CN V arises from the lateral pons as a large sensory root and a small motor root. The **trigeminal (semilunar/Gasserian) ganglion** lies in **Meckel's cave**, a dural pocket over the petrous apex. Three divisions leave it.

**V1, ophthalmic.** It runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus and enters the orbit through the **superior orbital fissure**. Its three branches:
- **Frontal**: supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves to the forehead and scalp, back to about the vertex.
- **Lacrimal**: lateral upper eyelid and lacrimal gland area.
- **Nasociliary**: cornea via the long ciliary nerves, plus the infratrochlear, the ethmoidal nerves and the external nasal branch to the nasal tip. The cornea is the afferent limb of the **corneal reflex**, and CN VII is the efferent limb.

**V2, maxillary.** It also runs in the cavernous sinus wall, low down, and exits through the **foramen rotundum** into the **pterygopalatine fossa**. Branches:
- **Infraorbital nerve**: runs through the orbital floor and emerges at the infraorbital foramen to supply the cheek, lower lid and upper lip.
- **Superior alveolar nerves** (posterior, middle, anterior): supply the upper teeth.
- **Greater and lesser palatine** and **nasopalatine** nerves: supply the palate and nasal cavity.
- **Zygomatic nerve**: zygomaticofacial and zygomaticotemporal branches.

**V3, mandibular.** It exits through the **foramen ovale** into the **infratemporal fossa**, outside the cavernous sinus.
- **Anterior trunk** (mostly motor): masseteric, deep temporal and lateral pterygoid nerves, plus the **buccal nerve**, which is sensory to the cheek mucosa.
- **Posterior trunk** (mostly sensory): the **auriculotemporal** nerve (which splits around the middle meningeal artery), the **lingual** nerve (general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue), and the **inferior alveolar** nerve. The inferior alveolar gives off the nerve to mylohyoid just before entering the mandibular foramen, and ends as the **mental nerve**.
- V3 motor supply: the muscles of mastication, plus mylohyoid, the anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.

The **angle of the jaw** is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2-C3), not by CN V. This is a useful clinical landmark.
levels.phd:
The three divisions reflect embryology. V1 supplies frontonasal-process territory. V2 and V3 supply the maxillary and mandibular prominences of the **first pharyngeal arch**. This is why V3 alone carries branchiomotor fibers: every first-arch muscle (mastication, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini) is innervated by V3.

**Dermatomal precision.** The V1/V2 border runs roughly along the palpebral fissure. The V2/V3 border runs along the oral commissure and up toward the temple. The territories overlap little at the midline but do overlap at their edges.

**Meninges.** CN V is the principal sensory nerve of the supratentorial dura:
- V1 gives the **tentorial nerve** (of Arnold).
- V2 and V3 supply the middle cranial fossa dura; V3 does so via the nervus spinosus, which travels with the middle meningeal artery through the foramen spinosum.

The posterior fossa dura is supplied mainly by upper cervical roots and the vagus. This trigeminovascular innervation underpins referred headache.

**Hitchhiking autonomics.** CN V carries no preganglionic parasympathetic fibers of its own, yet its branches distribute postganglionic fibers from the head's parasympathetic ganglia:
- The zygomatic and lacrimal nerves carry secretomotor fibers to the lacrimal gland, coming from the pterygopalatine ganglion.
- The auriculotemporal nerve carries fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid.
- The lingual nerve carries chorda tympani fibers (taste and submandibular secretomotor).

The ganglia themselves belong to a later lesson.

**Central organization.** Primary afferents in the ganglion project to:
- the principal sensory nucleus (discriminative touch);
- the **spinal trigeminal nucleus**, which descends to about C2-C3 (pain and temperature);
- the mesencephalic nucleus, which uniquely contains the cell bodies of muscle-spindle afferents that skip the ganglion.

The spinal nucleus has an **onion-skin** somatotopy: perioral zones map rostrally and peripheral facial zones caudally. This explains concentric facial numbness in lesions of the upper cervical cord or medulla, not divisional numbness.

**Controversy.** The traditional view holds that V2 is "purely sensory." Debate persists over the exact contributions of buccal versus long buccal fibers and accessory dental innervation, for example the mylohyoid nerve supplying the mandibular incisors. This matters clinically when inferior alveolar blocks fail.
levels.expert:
**Localization by pattern** is the clinical payoff.
- **Isolated mental nerve numbness** ("numb chin syndrome") is a red flag. It can signal metastatic disease to the mandible or skull base, or lymphoma, and warrants imaging.
- Numbness in the **infraorbital** distribution follows orbital floor (blowout) and zygomaticomaxillary fractures.
- Combined V1 + V2 deficit with ophthalmoplegia localizes to the **cavernous sinus** or superior orbital fissure. Adding optic involvement points to the orbital apex.
- A V3 deficit with jaw deviation toward the lesion on opening (ipsilateral pterygoid weakness) suggests a foramen ovale or infratemporal process.
- **Perineural spread**, classically from cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma or adenoid cystic carcinoma, tracks centripetally along V2 and V3 through the rotundum and ovale toward Meckel's cave. It needs contrast-enhanced, fat-suppressed MRI, and it changes resection and radiation fields.

**Trigeminal neuralgia.** Classical cases usually involve V2 and/or V3 and rarely V1 alone. They mostly reflect neurovascular compression at the root entry zone, most often by the superior cerebellar artery. Microvascular decompression addresses that cause.

Percutaneous procedures exploit peripheral anatomy:
- A needle passes through the cheek to the **foramen ovale** using the Härtel technique, for radiofrequency rhizotomy, glycerol, or balloon compression. Balloon compression can provoke a trigeminocardiac (vagal) reflex.
- Stereotactic radiosurgery targets the cisternal root.
- A key pitfall is corneal anesthesia: if V1 sensation is lost, the cornea is at risk of **neurotrophic keratopathy**, so V1-sparing lesions are preferred.

**Surgical windows.**
- The anterolateral and anteromedial middle-fossa triangles lie between the divisions; these are the Mullan and Kawase-region corridors.
- In endoscopic endonasal work, the vidian canal and V2 at the foramen rotundum serve as landmarks to the petrous carotid and Meckel's cave.
- In the infratemporal fossa, the lingual nerve lies close to the third molar, making it vulnerable during extraction.

**Open questions.**
- Ganglion-targeted approaches are being refined: CGRP biology from the trigeminovascular system has already produced migraine therapies.
- Diffusion tractography of the cisternal root is being studied as a way to predict surgical outcomes.
- Mechanisms of anesthesia dolorosa after ablation remain poorly understood.

keyPoints: CN V has three divisions: V1 ophthalmic, V2 maxillary, V3 mandibular
Exits: V1 superior orbital fissure, V2 foramen rotundum, V3 foramen ovale
V1 and V2 are sensory; V3 also carries motor fibers to first-arch muscles
Ganglion sits in Meckel's cave; V1 and V2 run in the cavernous sinus wall
Angle of the jaw is supplied by the great auricular nerve, not CN V
Patterns like numb chin or Hutchinson's sign localize disease

test.q: Which trigeminal division exits the skull through the foramen rotundum?
test.explain: V2 (maxillary) passes through the foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa. V3 uses the foramen ovale.

test.q: Which division carries motor fibers to the muscles of mastication?
test.explain: Only V3 is mixed, supplying first-arch muscles such as masseter and temporalis.

test.q: Skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by:
test.explain: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) supplies this area. It is a classic exception to trigeminal territory.

test.q: Hutchinson's sign (a rash on the nasal tip in shingles) predicts eye involvement because of which nerve?
test.explain: The nasociliary branch supplies both the nasal tip (external nasal branch) and the cornea.

test.q: General sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travels in the:
test.explain: The lingual nerve (V3) carries general sensation. Taste rides along with it from the chorda tympani.

test.q: The trigeminal ganglion lies within a dural pocket called:
test.explain: Meckel's cave sits over the petrous apex. V1 and V2 then run forward in the cavernous sinus wall.

test.q: A blowout fracture of the orbital floor most likely numbs the:
choices: Skin in front of the ear
test.explain: The infraorbital nerve (V2) runs in the orbital floor and supplies the cheek, lower lid and upper lip.

test.q: The sensory (afferent) limb of the corneal reflex is carried by:
test.explain: V1 provides corneal sensation via the long ciliary nerves. CN VII is the efferent (blink) limb.

test.q: Which nerve ends as the mental nerve?
test.explain: The inferior alveolar nerve runs in the mandibular canal and emerges at the mental foramen as the mental nerve.

test.q: V3 leaves the skull through the foramen ___.
test.explain: The mnemonic 'Standing Room Only' gives the order: superior orbital fissure, rotundum, ovale.

test.q: What is the cranial nerve number of the trigeminal nerve (Roman numeral)?
test.explain: The trigeminal is cranial nerve V.

test.q: V1 enters the orbit through the superior orbital ___.
test.explain: The ophthalmic division passes through the superior orbital fissure.

kidTest.q: How many big branches does the trigeminal nerve have?
kidTest.explain: 'Tri' means three.

kidTest.q: Which branch feels your forehead?
kidTest.explain: The top branch covers the forehead and eyes.

kidTest.q: Which branch helps you chew?
kidTest.explain: The bottom branch moves the chewing muscles.

kidTest.q: Your cheek and top teeth are felt by the:
kidTest.explain: The middle branch covers cheeks, nose and top teeth.

kidTest.q: The trigeminal nerve mostly helps your f _ _ _ feel things.
kidTest.explain: It is the main feeling nerve of the face.

advancedTest.q: A lesion of the upper cervical cord involving the spinal trigeminal nucleus produces facial numbness that is most likely:
choices: Divisional, involving V2 and V3 together
Limited to the anterior tongue and lower lip
Confined to the V1 dermatome on that side
advancedTest.explain: Onion-skin somatotopy maps peripheral face caudally, giving concentric loss that spares the mouth. A peripheral lesion would give divisional loss.

advancedTest.q: Numbness of V1 and V2 with ophthalmoplegia but normal V3 best localizes to the:
advancedTest.explain: V1 and V2 run in the lateral cavernous sinus wall with the ocular motor nerves. V3 exits below and lies outside it.

advancedTest.q: During percutaneous rhizotomy, sparing V1 is preferred mainly to avoid:
choices: Loss of taste on the anterior tongue
advancedTest.explain: V1 supplies the cornea; losing that sensation removes protective reflexes and risks neurotrophic keratopathy. Masseter is supplied by V3 and the mandibular angle by C2-C3.

advancedTest.q: Why does V3 alone innervate tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini?
choices: Both derive from the first pharyngeal arch
Both receive fibers from the otic ganglion
Both lie within the pterygopalatine fossa
Both muscles share a blood supply with the masseter
advancedTest.explain: V3 is the nerve of the first arch, so it supplies every first-arch muscle. The otic ganglion is autonomic, not branchiomotor.

lessons.title: Intratemporal Facial Nerve: Geniculate Ganglion, Greater Petrosal & Chorda Tympani

levels.kid:
Your face has a special nerve called the **facial nerve**. It works like a long electric cable from your brain to your face. It lets you smile, blink and wrinkle your nose.

Before it reaches your face, the cable travels through a twisty tunnel inside the bone near your ear. Inside that tunnel, it splits off a few smaller wires, like branches off a tree.

- One wire helps your eyes make **tears**.
- One tiny wire tightens a little muscle in your ear so loud sounds don't hurt as much.
- One wire, the **chorda tympani**, carries **taste** from the front of your tongue and helps make spit.

So one nerve helps you smile, cry, hear gently and taste candy!
levels.hs:
The **facial nerve** is cranial nerve VII (CN VII). Most people know it moves the muscles of facial expression, but it also carries taste, controls tear and saliva glands, and protects the ear from loud sound.

CN VII leaves the brainstem and enters the skull through the **internal acoustic meatus**. It then runs through a narrow bony tunnel in the temporal bone called the **facial canal**. This is the longest bony canal that any nerve travels through, about 3 cm. It finally exits the skull at the **stylomastoid foramen**, behind the jaw.

Inside the temporal bone, three key branches leave:
- **Greater petrosal nerve**: carries signals to the **lacrimal gland** (tears) and glands in the nose and palate.
- **Nerve to stapedius**: supplies the **stapedius**, the smallest skeletal muscle in the body. It damps vibration of the stapes bone when sounds are loud.
- **Chorda tympani**: crosses the middle ear, then joins the lingual nerve. It carries **taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue** and drives the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands.

A bend in the canal holds the **geniculate ganglion**, a cluster of sensory nerve cell bodies for taste.

Real example: in **Bell's palsy**, the nerve swells inside its tight canal. Patients may lose facial movement on one side, and some also notice altered taste or sounds that seem too loud.
levels.college:
CN VII has two roots: the motor root and the smaller **nervus intermedius**, which carries taste, general sensory and parasympathetic fibers. Both enter the **internal acoustic meatus** with CN VIII and travel in the facial (fallopian) canal in three segments:

- **Labyrinthine segment**: the shortest (about 3–5 mm) and narrowest part of the canal. It runs anterolaterally between the cochlea and the vestibule.
- **Geniculum** (first genu): a sharp backward turn that houses the **geniculate ganglion**. This holds pseudounipolar cell bodies for taste (special visceral afferent) and a small area of general sensation from the ear. No synapses occur here.
- **Tympanic (horizontal) segment**: runs posteriorly along the medial wall of the middle ear, above the oval window. Its bony covering is often thin or missing.
- **Second genu and mastoid (vertical) segment**: descends to the **stylomastoid foramen**.

**Branches, proximal to distal:**
- **Greater petrosal nerve** leaves at the geniculate ganglion. It carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the superior salivatory nucleus. It exits through the hiatus for the greater petrosal nerve and runs across the middle cranial fossa floor. It then joins the **deep petrosal nerve** (sympathetic) to form the **nerve of the pterygoid canal** (vidian nerve). Its targets are the lacrimal, nasal and palatine glands, and it also carries palatal taste.
- **Nerve to stapedius** arises from the mastoid segment.
- **Chorda tympani** usually leaves the mastoid segment a few millimetres above the stylomastoid foramen. It crosses the tympanic membrane medial to the handle of the malleus. It exits through the **petrotympanic fissure** and joins the **lingual nerve (V3)**. It carries anterior two-thirds taste and preganglionic fibers to the **submandibular ganglion**.

Lesion level predicts symptoms. A lesion above the geniculate ganglion can cause dry eye, hyperacusis, taste loss and facial palsy. A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen causes facial palsy alone.
levels.phd:
The intratemporal course reflects second-pharyngeal-arch origin. CN VII is the arch II nerve, so it supplies the stapedius and the other arch II muscles. The chorda tympani is classically described as a pretrematic branch that passes into arch I territory, which explains its joining the lingual nerve.

**Functional components.** The motor root carries special visceral efferent fibers from the facial motor nucleus. These fibers loop dorsally around the abducens nucleus as the internal genu, forming the facial colliculus. The nervus intermedius carries three kinds of fibers:
- General visceral efferent fibers from the superior salivatory nucleus.
- Special visceral afferent taste fibers, which enter the rostral nucleus tractus solitarius.
- General somatic afferent fibers from the concha and external canal, which project to the spinal trigeminal nucleus.

Taste cell bodies sit in the geniculate ganglion. The postganglionic parasympathetic cell bodies lie outside the temporal bone, in the pterygopalatine and submandibular ganglia.

**Bottleneck physiology.** The labyrinthine segment has the narrowest canal diameter, often cited as below about 0.7 mm at the meatal foramen. In this segment the nerve fills most of the lumen, and the blood supply is a watershed zone. The petrosal branch of the middle meningeal artery supplies it from above, and the stylomastoid artery supplies it from below. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI in Bell's palsy typically shows enhancement of the labyrinthine segment and geniculate ganglion. This supports compression, ischemia and edema at the meatal foramen as central to the disease, with HSV-1 reactivation the leading proposed trigger. The causal role of HSV-1 remains debated.

**Topognostic testing.** Clinicians use tests to locate a lesion along the nerve:
- The **Schirmer test** checks greater petrosal function.
- The **stapedial reflex** checks the nerve to stapedius.
- **Electrogustometry** and salivary flow check the chorda tympani.

These tests were historically used to localize lesions. However, nerve fibers within the trunk are not neatly separated, and lesions are often patchy, so the results correlate imperfectly with lesion site. They are now considered of limited reliability.

**Taste convergence.** Chorda tympani signals inhibit glossopharyngeal taste input centrally. Chorda tympani section can cause phantom taste or heightened posterior-tongue sensation. This is consistent with Bartoshuk's release-of-inhibition model.
levels.expert:
Surgical relevance centers on predictable danger points.

**Middle ear and mastoid surgery.** The tympanic segment has natural bony gaps (dehiscences), most often above the oval window. Temporal bone studies report dehiscence in a substantial minority of specimens, with series ranging up to about half. Surgeons therefore treat the facial nerve as possibly exposed during stapes surgery, and a prolapsing nerve can overhang the footplate. In mastoidectomy, the key landmarks are:
- The lateral semicircular canal, the short process of the incus and the digastric ridge locate the second genu and the mastoid segment.
- The **facial recess** is a window bounded by the facial nerve, the chorda tympani and the fossa incudis. Opening it (posterior tympanotomy) is the standard route for cochlear implant electrodes. Sacrificing the chorda gives wider access but costs taste.

Continuous facial nerve EMG monitoring is routine in these operations.

**Skull base.** In the middle fossa approach, the greater petrosal nerve is traced backward to find the geniculate ganglion. Surgeons must avoid traction on it, because pulling it can stretch the geniculate ganglion. Bare GSPN can lie over an exposed geniculate in some patients. Vestibular schwannoma surgery threatens the nerve's canalicular course. Outcomes are graded with the House–Brackmann scale.

**Temporal bone fractures.** Otic-capsule-violating fractures injure the nerve more often than sparing ones. The perigeniculate region is the most commonly injured site. When paralysis is immediate and complete, electroneuronography showing more than 90% degeneration within the first two weeks is the classic trigger to consider decompression. The evidence base remains largely retrospective.

**Bell's palsy decompression** through the middle fossa, targeting the meatal foramen, is controversial. The 2013 AAO-HNS guideline makes no recommendation for or against surgical decompression.

**Aberrant regeneration.** Misdirected regrowth of fibers after injury produces recognizable syndromes:
- **Crocodile tears**: lacrimation while eating, from salivary fibers rerouted into the greater petrosal pathway.
- **Synkinesis**: unintended movements that occur alongside voluntary facial movements.

Botulinum toxin and neuromuscular retraining help manage synkinesis.

**Imaging.** Thin-section CT shows the canal and any dehiscences. A geniculate hemangioma or a facial nerve schwannoma that enlarges the canal is an important mimic of refractory palsy. Progressive palsy beyond about 3 weeks or 6 months without recovery demands imaging.

keyPoints: CN VII runs ~3 cm through the facial canal from internal acoustic meatus to stylomastoid foramen
Labyrinthine segment is the narrowest point, a key site in Bell's palsy
Geniculate ganglion holds taste cell bodies; no synapses occur there
Greater petrosal nerve: parasympathetic to lacrimal, nasal and palatine glands via vidian nerve
Nerve to stapedius damps loud sound; loss causes hyperacusis
Chorda tympani: anterior two-thirds taste and submandibular/sublingual secretion via lingual nerve

test.q: Where does the facial nerve leave the skull to reach the face?
test.explain: CN VII exits at the stylomastoid foramen. Foramen ovale carries V3, and the jugular foramen carries IX–XI.

test.q: Which gland is controlled by the greater petrosal nerve pathway?
test.explain: Greater petrosal fibers drive tear secretion via the pterygopalatine ganglion. The submandibular gland is served by the chorda tympani.

test.q: The chorda tympani carries taste from which region?
test.explain: Chorda tympani carries anterior two-thirds taste. The posterior third is served by CN IX.

test.q: Which nerve does the chorda tympani join after leaving the skull?
test.explain: It exits through the petrotympanic fissure and joins the lingual nerve, a branch of V3.

test.q: What does the geniculate ganglion mainly contain?
test.explain: It holds pseudounipolar sensory cell bodies. Parasympathetic synapses happen in the pterygopalatine and submandibular ganglia.

test.q: Loss of the nerve to stapedius most typically causes:
test.explain: Stapedius damps stapes motion; paralysis produces hyperacusis.

test.q: Which segment of the facial canal is the narrowest?
test.explain: The labyrinthine segment is the narrowest part of the canal, making it a likely site of compression in Bell's palsy.

test.q: A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen would cause:
test.explain: All three intratemporal branches leave above the foramen, so taste, tears and hearing are spared.

test.q: The greater petrosal nerve joins the deep petrosal nerve to form the:
test.explain: Together they form the vidian nerve (nerve of the pterygoid canal), which runs to the pterygopalatine ganglion.

test.q: The smaller root of CN VII that carries taste and parasympathetic fibers is the nervus ___.
test.explain: The nervus intermedius carries taste, general sensory and parasympathetic fibers.

test.q: What is the smallest skeletal muscle in the body, supplied by a branch of CN VII?
test.explain: The stapedius attaches to the stapes and damps loud sounds.

test.q: The chorda tympani exits the skull through the petrotympanic ___.
test.explain: The petrotympanic fissure transmits the chorda tympani out of the temporal bone.

kidTest.q: What does the facial nerve help you do?
kidTest.explain: It moves the muscles of your face.

kidTest.q: Where does the facial nerve travel through a twisty tunnel?
choices: In the bone of your arm
In the bone near your ear
In the bone of your knee
kidTest.explain: The tunnel is in the bone beside your ear.

kidTest.q: The chorda tympani wire carries which sense?
kidTest.explain: It carries taste from the front of the tongue.

kidTest.q: One branch helps your eyes make what?
kidTest.explain: A branch tells the tear gland to make tears.

kidTest.q: A tiny muscle helps calm loud sounds. Sounds go into your e _ _ first.
kidTest.explain: Sounds enter the ear, where a tiny muscle softens them.

advancedTest.q: Bell's palsy MRI enhancement concentrates at the labyrinthine segment and geniculate ganglion. The best explanation is:
choices: The narrow canal plus watershed blood supply makes edema compressive there
The canal is widest there, letting fluid pool around the nerve
Taste fibers are especially vulnerable to herpes virus in the mastoid
The stapedius nerve originates there and drives inflammation upward
advancedTest.explain: The labyrinthine segment is the narrowest part of the canal and a vascular watershed, so swelling causes compression and ischemia there.

advancedTest.q: A patient has facial palsy, hyperacusis and taste loss, but tear production is normal. The lesion is most likely:
choices: Proximal to the geniculate ganglion itself
At the stylomastoid foramen exit point
Within the parotid gland near the face
advancedTest.explain: Greater petrosal is spared, but stapedius and chorda tympani are lost, placing the lesion distal to the geniculate and proximal to the stapedius branch.

advancedTest.q: Why are crocodile tears (tearing while eating) seen after facial nerve injury?
choices: Sympathetic fibers from the deep petrosal take over taste
Salivary fibers regrow into the greater petrosal pathway
Chorda tympani fibers trigger direct lacrimal reflexes
Stapedius denervation raises pressure in the lacrimal sac
advancedTest.explain: Aberrant regeneration sends salivary secretomotor fibers into the lacrimal pathway, so eating causes tearing.

advancedTest.q: During posterior tympanotomy for a cochlear implant, enlarging access by sacrificing a boundary structure most typically costs:
advancedTest.explain: The facial recess is bounded by the facial nerve and chorda tympani; dividing the chorda widens access at the cost of taste.

lessons.title: Glossopharyngeal, Vagus & Accessory Nerves in the Neck

levels.kid:
Inside your head there are 12 pairs of special wires called **cranial nerves**. Three of them leave the skull through the same little door, a hole called the **jugular foramen**. Their names are number 9, number 10 and number 11.

Number 9 helps you taste with the very back of your tongue and helps you swallow.

Number 10 is the longest traveler. It is called the **vagus**, which means "wanderer." It goes all the way down to your heart, lungs and tummy. It also helps you talk.

Number 11 moves two big muscles. One turns your head. The other lets you shrug your shoulders.

Surgeons learn exactly where these wires run so they can keep them safe.
levels.hs:
Cranial nerves IX, X and XI all leave the skull through the **jugular foramen**, a gap next to the internal jugular vein. In the neck they spread out to very different jobs.

**Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)** ("tongue-throat"):
- Taste and general sensation from the back third of the tongue
- Sensation from the throat (pharynx), which starts the **gag reflex**
- Moves one throat muscle, the **stylopharyngeus**, which lifts the throat when you swallow
- Sends a branch to the **carotid sinus**, a pressure sensor in the carotid artery

**Vagus nerve (CN X)** ("wandering"):
- Runs down the neck inside the **carotid sheath**, a tube of tissue around the carotid artery and jugular vein
- Moves most muscles of the throat and voice box (larynx)
- Carries parasympathetic, "rest and digest" signals to the heart, lungs and gut

**Accessory nerve (CN XI)**:
- Moves the **sternocleidomastoid** (turns the head) and the **trapezius** (shrugs the shoulder)

A real example: during thyroid surgery, surgeons protect a vagus branch called the **recurrent laryngeal nerve**. If it is injured, the vocal cord on that side stops moving and the voice becomes hoarse.
levels.college:
**Exit.** CN IX, X and XI leave through the **jugular foramen**. IX lies anteromedial. X and XI travel with the internal jugular vein. IX and X each carry two sensory ganglia, a superior and an inferior one. The inferior vagal ganglion is also called the **nodose ganglion**.

**CN IX in the neck:**
- Descends between the internal carotid artery and the internal jugular vein, then curves forward around **stylopharyngeus**, the only muscle it supplies
- Passes between the superior and middle constrictors to reach the posterior third of the tongue (taste and general sensation)
- **Carotid sinus nerve** (baroreceptors) and **carotid body** (chemoreceptors)
- Pharyngeal branches join the **pharyngeal plexus**. IX forms the afferent limb of the gag reflex, and X forms the efferent limb.
- **Tympanic nerve** (Jacobson's) leads, via the lesser petrosal nerve, to the otic ganglion and on to the parotid gland

**CN X in the neck:**
- Runs in the carotid sheath, posterior to and between the internal jugular vein and the carotid artery
- **Auricular branch** (Arnold's): ear canal sensation. Stimulating it can trigger the ear-cough reflex.
- **Pharyngeal branch**: supplies all pharyngeal and palatal muscles except stylopharyngeus and tensor veli palatini
- **Superior laryngeal nerve**: its internal branch is sensory above the vocal folds. Its external branch supplies cricothyroid and runs beside the superior thyroid artery.
- **Recurrent laryngeal nerve**: hooks under the subclavian artery on the right and the aortic arch on the left, then rises in the tracheoesophageal groove. It supplies all other intrinsic laryngeal muscles and sensation below the folds.
- Cardiac branches

**CN XI:**
- Supplies sternocleidomastoid, then crosses the **posterior triangle** superficially, on levator scapulae, to reach trapezius
- Its superficial course makes it vulnerable during lymph node biopsy. Injury causes shoulder droop and lateral scapular winging.
levels.phd:
**Jugular foramen compartments.** Classic descriptions split the foramen into a pars nervosa (IX, with the inferior petrosal sinus) and a pars vascularis (X, XI and the sigmoid-jugular bulb). Modern microsurgical work, notably Rhoton's, describes **intrajugular septa** separating a petrosal part, a sigmoid part and an intrajugular part that carries the nerves. Tumor displacement patterns follow these partitions.

**Functional components.** CN IX and X share brainstem nuclei:
- **Nucleus ambiguus**: branchial motor fibers
- **Inferior salivatory nucleus**: IX parasympathetic fibers
- **Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus**: preganglionic fibers to the viscera. Cardiac vagal output arises largely from nucleus ambiguus neurons.
- **Nucleus tractus solitarius**: receives visceral afferents and taste

Vagal afferents outnumber efferents by roughly 4:1, and the majority of vagal axons are unmyelinated C fibers. The nodose ganglion holds the cell bodies of visceral afferents, including baroreceptor afferents from the aortic arch. Carotid sinus afferents travel in IX via Hering's nerve.

**Carotid body.** Type I glomus cells sense hypoxia. Low O2 inhibits K+ channels, which depolarizes the cell and opens Ca2+ channels. ATP is released onto P2X2/3 receptors on petrosal afferents. Mitochondrial complex I signalling and hypoxia-sensitive TASK channels are implicated, though the exact oxygen sensor remains debated.

**Recurrent laryngeal asymmetry.** The asymmetry is embryological. The nerves hook under the 6th arch arteries. On the right, the distal 6th and dorsal 5th arch vessels regress, so the nerve rises to the 4th arch derivative, the subclavian artery. On the left, it stays under the ductus arteriosus or ligamentum arteriosum. If the right subclavian artery is aberrant (arteria lusoria), a **non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve** occurs in about 0.5-1% of people.

**Accessory nerve.** The "cranial root" is now widely regarded as aberrant vagal fibers, so CN XI is essentially the spinal accessory nerve. It arises from the upper cervical cord (about C1-C5/6), ascends through the foramen magnum, then exits via the jugular foramen. Cervical plexus contributions (C2-C4) to trapezius are mainly proprioceptive, which explains variable deficits after section.
levels.expert:
**Skull-base syndromes localize the lesion.**
- **Vernet syndrome** (IX, X, XI): a lesion at the jugular foramen, such as a glomus jugulare paraganglioma or schwannoma.
- **Collet-Sicard syndrome** adds XII palsy, pointing to the condylar or retrostyloid region.
- **Villaret syndrome** adds Horner syndrome, implicating the retrostyloid (poststyloid parapharyngeal) space, where the sympathetic chain lies near the internal carotid artery.
- Examination signs: uvula deviates toward the intact side; on the affected side the pharyngeal wall pulls toward the normal side (the curtain sign); ipsilateral shoulder droop and weak head turning to the opposite side.

**Paragangliomas.** Carotid body tumors splay the internal and external carotid arteries (the lyre sign). Vagal paragangliomas push the carotid anteromedially. Succinate dehydrogenase (SDHx) germline variants, especially SDHD, are frequent, so genetic testing and screening for multifocal disease are standard. Vagal tumors often cause vocal fold palsy after resection, which drives active surveillance or radiosurgery for selected cases.

**Thyroid and anterior cervical spine surgery.**
- Intraoperative nerve monitoring helps detect loss of signal. Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy can cause airway obstruction, so many surgeons stage the second side after loss of signal.
- In the anterior cervical (ACDF) approach, a dysphonia risk is debated. The left-sided approach is often favored because the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is longer and more predictable, though randomized data have not shown a clear side difference.
- External branch injury lowers pitch range, which matters greatly for singers.

**Spinal accessory nerve.** Injury is one of the most common iatrogenic nerve injuries. Erb's point, where great auricular emerges, is a key landmark; XI emerges about 1 cm above it. Selective neck dissection preserving XI has largely replaced radical dissection to reduce shoulder dysfunction. Repair options include direct repair or a nerve transfer.

**Neuromodulation.** Cervical vagus nerve stimulation, placed on the left to limit cardiac effects via the right vagus and sinoatrial node, is approved for drug-resistant epilepsy and depression. It is also used for stroke rehabilitation (paired VNS, FDA 2021). Cough, hoarseness and dyspnea reflect stimulation of laryngeal efferents. An open question is fiber-selective stimulation of afferent fibers to separate therapeutic effects from off-target ones. **Glossopharyngeal neuralgia**, sometimes with vagal syncope, is treated by microvascular decompression, often of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA).

keyPoints: CN IX, X and XI all exit the skull through the jugular foramen
CN IX: taste on the posterior third of the tongue, stylopharyngeus, carotid sinus and carotid body
Gag reflex: CN IX afferent, CN X efferent
The vagus runs in the carotid sheath and supplies most pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles
The right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the subclavian artery; the left hooks under the aortic arch
CN XI supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius and is vulnerable in the posterior triangle

test.q: Which opening do cranial nerves IX, X and XI share to leave the skull?
test.explain: All three pass through the jugular foramen. The hypoglossal canal carries CN XII.

test.q: What is the only muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve?
test.explain: Stylopharyngeus is supplied by CN IX. Palatoglossus and levator veli palatini are vagal, and cricothyroid is supplied by the external laryngeal branch of the vagus.

test.q: In the gag reflex, which nerve carries the sensory (afferent) limb?
test.explain: CN IX senses the pharynx (afferent limb), and CN X contracts the pharyngeal muscles (efferent limb).

test.q: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops beneath which structure?
test.explain: The left nerve hooks under the aortic arch near the ligamentum arteriosum. The right one hooks under the subclavian artery.

test.q: Which laryngeal muscle is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve?
test.explain: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies cricothyroid. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the other intrinsic muscles.

test.q: Injury to the accessory nerve in the posterior triangle most likely causes:
test.explain: The trapezius is weakened, so the shoulder droops. Hoarseness points to the vagus, and tongue deviation to CN XII.

test.q: Within the carotid sheath, the vagus lies:
test.explain: The vagus sits posteriorly in the groove between the internal jugular vein and the carotid artery.

test.q: Carotid sinus pressure signals reach the brainstem mainly via:
test.explain: The carotid sinus nerve (Hering's nerve) is a branch of CN IX.

test.q: The auricular (Arnold's) branch of the vagus explains which reflex?
test.explain: Stimulating the ear canal, which this branch supplies, can provoke coughing.

test.q: What is the vagal branch that runs in the tracheoesophageal groove called?
test.explain: The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove to reach the larynx.

test.q: CN IX carries taste from the posterior one-___ of the tongue.
test.explain: The glossopharyngeal nerve covers the posterior third of the tongue for taste and general sensation.

test.q: What is the name of the inferior sensory ganglion of the vagus?
test.explain: The inferior vagal ganglion is called the nodose ganglion. It holds the cell bodies of visceral afferents.

kidTest.q: What does the name 'vagus' mean?
kidTest.explain: The vagus wanders far, all the way down to the heart, lungs and tummy.

kidTest.q: Nerve number 11 helps you:
kidTest.explain: It moves the trapezius muscle, which shrugs the shoulders, and the muscle that turns your head.

kidTest.q: Nerve number 9 helps you taste with which part of your tongue?
kidTest.explain: Nerve 9 handles taste from the back of the tongue.

kidTest.q: How do nerves 9, 10 and 11 leave the skull?
choices: Each one through its own hole
kidTest.explain: All three share one door, called the jugular foramen.

kidTest.q: The vagus nerve reaches the h _ _ _ _, the organ that pumps blood.
kidTest.explain: The vagus travels down to the heart, lungs and tummy.

advancedTest.q: A patient has palsies of CN IX, X and XI plus a Horner syndrome. The lesion most likely lies in the:
advancedTest.explain: This is Villaret syndrome. The sympathetic chain lies near the lower cranial nerves in the retrostyloid space. A lesion confined to the jugular foramen would spare the sympathetic chain.

advancedTest.q: A non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve is predicted by which finding?
advancedTest.explain: With arteria lusoria there is no normal right 4th-arch vessel for the nerve to hook under, so it passes directly to the larynx.

advancedTest.q: Why is cervical vagus nerve stimulation usually placed on the left side?
choices: The left vagus has fewer afferent fibers
The right vagus carries no laryngeal fibers
The left vagus lies outside the carotid sheath
The right vagus more strongly drives the sinoatrial node
advancedTest.explain: Right vagal output preferentially affects the sinoatrial node, so left-sided stimulation lowers the risk of bradycardia.

advancedTest.q: Trapezius weakness after spinal accessory nerve section varies between patients mainly because:
choices: The vagus supplies the lower trapezius
The cranial root rescues trapezius function
C2-C4 plexus fibers sometimes carry motor input
advancedTest.explain: Cervical plexus contributions are mainly proprioceptive but variably motor, so deficits differ. The cranial root joins the vagus rather than supplying trapezius.

lessons.title: Hypoglossal Nerve, Ansa Cervicalis & the Cervical Plexus

levels.kid:
Your tongue is a busy muscle. It helps you talk, chew and swallow. A special wire from your brain, called the **hypoglossal nerve**, tells it how to move.

This nerve leaves the back of your skull through its own little tunnel. Then it curves down your neck and swings forward under your jaw to reach your tongue, like a hook.

Your neck also has a bundle of wires called the **cervical plexus**. Think of it like a power strip. Some wires make the skin of your neck and ear feel touch. One wire loop, called the **ansa**, moves the thin strap muscles in the front of your neck. Another wire, the phrenic nerve, runs all the way down to help you breathe!
levels.hs:
The **hypoglossal nerve** is cranial nerve XII (12). It is a **motor nerve**, meaning it controls muscles rather than carrying feeling. It moves almost all the muscles of the tongue. The one exception is the palatoglossus, which is supplied by the vagus nerve.

CN XII leaves the skull through the **hypoglossal canal**, just above the edge of the hole where the spinal cord exits. It drops down the neck between the big artery and vein, loops forward around the occipital artery, and crosses the carotid arteries before entering the tongue.

The **cervical plexus** is a network formed by the front branches of spinal nerves **C1 to C4**. It has two kinds of branches:
- **Sensory (cutaneous) branches** that supply the skin of the neck, the back of the scalp and part of the ear.
- **Motor branches**, including the **ansa cervicalis** (a nerve loop that supplies the flat "strap muscles" in front of the voice box) and the **phrenic nerve** (C3, C4, C5), which controls the diaphragm.

A real example: if one hypoglossal nerve is damaged, the tongue **points toward the injured side** when the person sticks it out. That happens because the healthy side pushes the tongue forward while the weak side cannot.
levels.college:
**Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).** Its fibres arise from the hypoglossal nucleus in the medulla and emerge between the pyramid and the olive. It exits through the **hypoglossal canal** in the occipital condyle. In the neck it:
- descends between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein, deep to the posterior belly of digastric;
- hooks around the **occipital artery** (near the origin of the sternocleidomastoid branch);
- crosses lateral to the internal and external carotid arteries and the loop of the lingual artery;
- runs on **hyoglossus**, superficial to it, with the lingual artery deep to that muscle. It lies below the submandibular duct and the lingual nerve.

It supplies all intrinsic tongue muscles plus genioglossus, hyoglossus and styloglossus. **Palatoglossus** is supplied by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus. A lower motor neuron lesion causes ipsilateral atrophy and fasciculations, and **deviation toward the lesion** on protrusion, because the intact genioglossus pushes unopposed.

**C1 hitchhikers.** Fibres from C1 join CN XII soon after it exits the skull. Some leave as the **superior root (descendens hypoglossi)** of the ansa cervicalis. Others continue with XII to supply **thyrohyoid** and **geniohyoid**.

**Ansa cervicalis.** The superior root (C1) joins the **inferior root** (C2–C3) to form a loop, usually lying on the carotid sheath. It supplies sternohyoid, sternothyroid and omohyoid.

**Cervical plexus (C1–C4 ventral rami).** It lies deep to sternocleidomastoid, on scalenus medius and levator scapulae.
- Cutaneous branches emerge at **Erb's point** (nerve point of the neck, mid-posterior border of SCM): lesser occipital (C2), great auricular (C2–C3), transverse cervical (C2–C3), and supraclavicular nerves (C3–C4).
- **Phrenic nerve** (C3–C5): descends on the anterior surface of scalenus anterior, deep to prevertebral fascia, into the thorax. It is the sole motor supply to its hemidiaphragm.
levels.phd:
**Nuclear and fascicular organization.** The hypoglossal nucleus forms the hypoglossal trigone in the floor of the fourth ventricle. Motor neurons are **myotopically organized**: dorsal subnuclei supply retrusors (hyoglossus, styloglossus) and ventral subnuclei supply the protrusor genioglossus. Corticobulbar input to genioglossus is predominantly **contralateral**. This explains why an upper motor neuron lesion, such as an internal capsule stroke, produces deviation **away** from the lesion, without atrophy. Rootlets traverse the medulla lateral to the medial lemniscus and pyramid. Medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome from anterior spinal or vertebral branch occlusion combines ipsilateral XII palsy with contralateral hemiparesis and loss of dorsal-column sensation.

**Embryology.** The tongue musculature derives from **occipital somites** (myotomes 2–4). Their migrating myoblasts form the hypoglossal cord, which carries CN XII ventrally and rostrally. This explains the nerve's descending-then-ascending hooked course and its somatic-efferent (GSE) classification, which links it to III, IV and VI rather than to the branchial nerves. The hypoglossal canal is often partly or fully bipartite, a vestige of the segmental (sclerotomal) origin of the occipital bone.

**Ansa variants.** The ansa lies anterior to the carotid sheath in most dissections, but it may sit within the sheath or deep to the IJV. Contributions from the vagus, or a C4 root, are reported. The inferior root may pass lateral or medial to the IJV, which bears on its exposure in neck dissection.

**Phrenic physiology.** C4 is usually dominant. An **accessory phrenic nerve**, usually from C5 via the nerve to subclavius, is present in roughly a quarter to a third of people. It can preserve diaphragmatic function after proximal phrenic injury and confound localization. Spinal cord injury at or above C3 abolishes spontaneous ventilation. Injury at C4–C5 produces variable dependence on a ventilator.

**Genioglossus and airway patency.** Genioglossus activity is driven by **phasic inspiratory input** from premotor neurons near the pre-Bötzinger complex, plus tonic serotonergic and noradrenergic drive. That wake-related drive falls in sleep, especially REM. Loss of genioglossus tone contributes to pharyngeal collapse in obstructive sleep apnoea, which is the physiological basis for hypoglossal nerve stimulation.
levels.expert:
**Hypoglossal nerve stimulation (HGNS).** Selective stimulation of protrusor branches (genioglossus) while sparing retrusor branches (hyoglossus, styloglossus) is now an established therapy for moderate-to-severe OSA in CPAP-intolerant patients. The landmark trial was **STAR** (Strollo et al., NEJM 2014, Inspire system). Surgeons map the distal branching pattern on hyoglossus and use EMG to confirm protrusion. Drug-induced sleep endoscopy screens out complete concentric velopharyngeal collapse, which predicts failure. Newer bilateral and implanted-sensorless devices aim to simplify the procedure. The anatomical pitfall is the **ranine veins** (venae comitantes of XII), which bleed readily during dissection.

**Skull-base and neck surgery.** The hypoglossal canal lies roughly at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds of the occipital condyle. In far-lateral transcondylar approaches, drilling beyond about the posterior third of the condyle risks the canal and craniocervical stability. Its venous plexus, which connects the marginal sinus and condylar veins, signals proximity. In **carotid endarterectomy**, XII crosses near the bifurcation and is injured in a small percentage of cases, usually by traction. Bilateral palsy after staged endarterectomies can produce dangerous airway and swallowing compromise. Surgeons therefore assess tongue function before operating on the second side.

**Hypoglossal schwannomas** are rare and dumbbell-shaped across the canal. **Isolated XII palsy** should prompt imaging of the canal and the craniocervical junction, including the high cervical ICA. Causes include carotid dissection, clival or condylar metastases, and glomus or jugular foramen lesions extending medially (Collet–Sicard syndrome when IX–XII are involved).

**Reinnervation surgery.** **Hypoglossal–facial anastomosis** remains a workhorse for facial reanimation after vestibular schwannoma resection. The end-to-side or split-nerve ("jump graft") variants limit hemitongue atrophy. The **ansa cervicalis–recurrent laryngeal nerve** transfer restores tone and bulk in unilateral vocal fold paralysis, though it does not restore abduction.

**Cervical plexus.** The superficial cervical plexus block is placed at Erb's point and is used for carotid endarterectomy and clavicle surgery. Phrenic involvement is relevant mainly with deep blocks and interscalene brachial plexus blocks, where hemidiaphragmatic paresis is common. Great auricular nerve sacrifice in parotidectomy leaves earlobe numbness. The nerve is also a convenient graft donor. Open questions include closed-loop HGNS and predictors of responder phenotypes.

keyPoints: CN XII is motor to all tongue muscles except palatoglossus (vagus)
XII exits the hypoglossal canal and hooks around the occipital artery to reach the tongue
LMN XII lesion: tongue deviates toward the lesion, with atrophy
Ansa cervicalis (C1 superior root + C2–C3 inferior root) supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles
Cervical plexus (C1–C4) gives cutaneous nerves at Erb's point
Phrenic nerve (C3–C5) on scalenus anterior supplies the diaphragm

lessons.title: Cervical Sympathetic Chain and the Ciliary, Pterygopalatine, Otic & Submandibular Ganglia

levels.kid:
Your body has a secret helper system that works without you thinking. It is called the **autonomic** system. It has two teams. One team, the "rush" team, gets you ready to run: big pupils, fast heart. The other team, the "rest" team, helps you relax, make tears and spit, and digest food.

In your neck there is a chain of little knots of nerves, like beads on a string. This is the rush team's chain for your head.

The rest team has four small relay stations in your head. They are called **ganglia**. One helps your eye. One helps tears and your nose. Two help make spit. Messages stop at these stations, like a bus changing drivers, and then travel on to do their jobs.
levels.hs:
The **autonomic nervous system** controls things you don't consciously steer, like pupil size, sweating, tears and saliva. It has two divisions. The **sympathetic** division handles "fight or flight." The **parasympathetic** division handles "rest and digest."

Each autonomic pathway uses two neurons. The first (**preganglionic**) neuron starts in the brainstem or spinal cord. It connects (synapses) with a second (**postganglionic**) neuron inside a cluster of nerve cell bodies called a **ganglion**.

**Sympathetic supply to the head** starts in the upper thoracic spinal cord, not the brain. Fibers climb up the **sympathetic chain** in the neck. That chain has three ganglia: superior, middle and inferior cervical. The **superior cervical ganglion** sends fibers along the carotid arteries to the eye, sweat glands and blood vessels of the face.

**Parasympathetic supply to the head** rides with four cranial nerves (III, VII, IX, X). The first three use four head ganglia:
- **Ciliary** ganglion (with CN III): pupil constriction and focusing.
- **Pterygopalatine** ganglion (with CN VII): tears and nasal glands.
- **Submandibular** ganglion (with CN VII): saliva from two glands under the jaw and tongue.
- **Otic** ganglion (with CN IX): saliva from the parotid gland.

A real example: damage to the sympathetic chain causes **Horner syndrome**. It produces a small pupil, a slightly droopy eyelid and reduced sweating on one side of the face.
levels.college:
**Cervical sympathetic chain.** Preganglionic sympathetic neurons for the head sit in the intermediolateral cell column of roughly T1-T2/T3. Their axons leave through white rami communicantes, enter the chain and ascend without synapsing. The chain lies on the prevertebral fascia, behind the carotid sheath.
- **Superior cervical ganglion** (C1-C4 level, near C2-C3): the largest. Postganglionic fibers form the **internal carotid plexus**, which supplies the dilator pupillae, superior tarsal (Müller) muscle and orbital vessels, and joins the deep petrosal nerve. The external carotid plexus carries fibers to facial sweat glands and vessels.
- **Middle cervical ganglion** (near C6): small and inconstant.
- **Inferior cervical ganglion** often fuses with T1 to form the **stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglion** in front of the neck of the first rib.
- Cervical ganglia send cardiac nerves to the cardiac plexus.

**Parasympathetic ganglia** (preganglionic nucleus → nerve → ganglion → target):
- **Ciliary**: Edinger-Westphal nucleus → CN III (inferior division, nerve to inferior oblique) → short ciliary nerves → sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle.
- **Pterygopalatine**: superior salivatory nucleus → nervus intermedius → greater petrosal nerve. This joins the deep petrosal nerve to form the **nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve)**. Targets are the lacrimal gland (via zygomatic branch of V2 and lacrimal nerve) and nasal, palatal and pharyngeal glands.
- **Submandibular**: superior salivatory nucleus → chorda tympani → lingual nerve → ganglion → submandibular and sublingual glands.
- **Otic**: inferior salivatory nucleus → CN IX → tympanic nerve (Jacobson) → tympanic plexus → lesser petrosal nerve → ganglion below the foramen ovale → auriculotemporal nerve (V3) → parotid.

Only parasympathetic fibers synapse in these ganglia. Sympathetic and sensory fibers pass through them. Trigeminal branches act as the "delivery trucks" that carry postganglionic fibers to their targets.
levels.phd:
**Neurochemistry.** Preganglionic neurons of both divisions release acetylcholine onto nicotinic (α3β4-containing) receptors in the ganglia. Postganglionic parasympathetic terminals act on muscarinic receptors: mostly M3 in the sphincter pupillae, ciliary muscle and salivary acini. Postganglionic sympathetic fibers release noradrenaline at α1 receptors in the dilator pupillae and Müller muscle. **Facial eccrine sweat glands are the exception**: they are sympathetically innervated but **cholinergic**, using muscarinic receptors. Co-transmitters matter. VIP from the pterygopalatine and otic ganglia drives vasodilation and fluid secretion, and nitric oxide from pterygopalatine neurons dilates cerebral and nasal vessels. This matters in cluster headache and nasal congestion.

**Horner syndrome localization.** The oculosympathetic pathway has three neurons.
- **First-order neurons** descend from the posterolateral hypothalamus through the lateral brainstem (e.g., lateral medullary/Wallenberg syndrome) to the ciliospinal centre of Budge (C8-T2).
- **Second-order neurons** pass over the lung apex. A Pancoast tumour is a classic lesion here.
- **Third-order neurons** run from the superior cervical ganglion along the internal carotid artery. Carotid dissection is a typical cause.

Ptosis is mild (1-2 mm) because only Müller muscle is lost. "Upside-down ptosis" comes from the denervated inferior tarsal muscle. Anhidrosis helps localize. Sudomotor fibers to most of the face follow the external carotid, so lesions above the bifurcation (third-order) usually spare facial sweating except a medial forehead strip. Anisocoria is greater in dim light, and the affected pupil shows **dilation lag**.

**Pharmacological testing.** Cocaine eye drops block noradrenaline reuptake. A Horner pupil, which receives little tonic noradrenaline, dilates poorly. Apraclonidine (a weak α1 agonist) reverses the anisocoria because the denervated dilator becomes supersensitive through α1 upregulation. Hydroxyamphetamine releases stored noradrenaline from intact third-order terminals. A failure to dilate therefore points to a postganglionic lesion.

**Development.** All four ganglia derive from neural crest. Lineage-tracing work (Dyachuk et al., Espinosa-Medina et al., 2014) showed that the parasympathetic ganglion neurons arise largely from nerve-associated Schwann cell precursors that migrate along the preganglionic nerves. This explains why the ganglia sit on their carrier nerves.
levels.expert:
**Adie tonic pupil** is a ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerve lesion, often post-viral. The pupil is large with segmental (vermiform) iris palsy. It shows light-near dissociation, because the near response reinnervates through many accommodative fibres (about 30:1 over pupillary fibres). Denervation supersensitivity makes it constrict to dilute pilocarpine. Holmes-Adie syndrome adds hyporeflexia. Contrast this with a compressive CN III palsy. Pupillomotor fibres run superficially and dorsomedially in the nerve, so a posterior communicating aneurysm classically produces an early fixed dilated pupil. Ischaemic microvascular palsies often spare the pupil.

**Painful Horner syndrome is carotid dissection until proven otherwise.** It needs urgent CTA or MRA of the head and neck. In children, think of neuroblastoma, and look for heterochromia if the lesion is congenital or early. Surgical Horner syndrome follows anterior cervical discectomy (from chain retraction over longus colli), carotid endarterectomy, thyroidectomy, chest tube or apical procedures, and stellate ganglion blocks. In neonates, think of brachial plexus birth injury.

**Pterygopalatine ganglion in practice.** The endoscopic endonasal approach uses the Vidian canal as a key landmark to the anterior genu of the petrous internal carotid artery. The vidian nerve is often sacrificed, which causes ipsilateral dry eye. Aberrant regeneration after facial palsy can produce **crocodile tears**, where salivatory fibres misroute to the lacrimal gland and cause tearing during eating. Ganglion stimulation is being studied as treatment for cluster headache, and the Pathway CH-1 trial reported acute attack relief. Neurostimulation of this ganglion is also being explored to augment cerebral blood flow in acute ischaemic stroke (ImpACT-24B).

**Frey syndrome** (gustatory sweating) follows parotidectomy. Severed otic postganglionic secretomotor fibres in the auriculotemporal nerve reinnervate cholinergic sweat glands of the skin. Starch-iodine (Minor) testing shows the affected area. Botulinum toxin, which blocks acetylcholine release, is effective. Placing a SMAS flap or other interposition tissue reduces the risk.

**Stellate ganglion block** is used for complex regional pain, refractory ventricular arrhythmia (cardiac sympathetic denervation) and, controversially, PTSD. Ipsilateral Horner syndrome confirms a successful block. Pitfalls include vertebral artery injection, recurrent laryngeal or phrenic nerve palsy, and pneumothorax.

**Open questions** include why cholinergic sympathetic sweat innervation exists, how ganglionic nitrergic signalling contributes to migraine, and how reliable cervical sympathetic chain preservation is in long-segment anterior spine surgery.

keyPoints: Autonomic pathways use two neurons that synapse in a ganglion
Head sympathetics arise from T1-T3 and ascend to the superior cervical ganglion
Ciliary (III), pterygopalatine (VII), submandibular (VII), otic (IX) are the parasympathetic head ganglia
Only parasympathetic fibers synapse in the four head ganglia; others pass through
Horner syndrome: miosis, mild ptosis, anhidrosis from oculosympathetic damage
Trigeminal branches carry postganglionic fibers to targets

test.q: Which ganglion supplies parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland?
test.explain: The otic ganglion receives lesser petrosal (CN IX) fibers and sends them via the auriculotemporal nerve to the parotid.

test.q: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons for the head are located in the:
test.explain: They lie in the intermediolateral column at about T1-T3 and ascend the chain to synapse in the cervical ganglia.

test.q: Which nerve carries preganglionic fibers to the ciliary ganglion?
test.explain: Fibers from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus travel in CN III, via the nerve to the inferior oblique.

test.q: The chorda tympani carries parasympathetic fibers to which ganglion?
test.explain: The chorda tympani joins the lingual nerve and synapses in the submandibular ganglion, which supplies the submandibular and sublingual glands.

test.q: Which set of signs defines Horner syndrome?
choices: Small pupil, mild ptosis, reduced sweating
Small pupil, eye turned out, dry mouth
Dilated pupil, double vision, facial droop
test.explain: Loss of sympathetic supply causes miosis, mild ptosis (Müller muscle) and anhidrosis. A dilated pupil with ptosis suggests CN III.

test.q: The inferior cervical ganglion often fuses with the first thoracic ganglion to form the:
test.explain: The stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglion lies in front of the neck of the first rib.

test.q: The greater petrosal and deep petrosal nerves join to form the:
test.explain: Together they form the Vidian nerve, which runs to the pterygopalatine ganglion.

test.q: Which fibers actually synapse in the four parasympathetic head ganglia?
test.explain: Sympathetic and sensory fibers pass through without synapsing. Only parasympathetic fibers relay there.

test.q: A Pancoast tumor at the lung apex causes Horner syndrome by damaging which neurons?
test.explain: Second-order (preganglionic) fibers arch over the lung apex on their way to the superior cervical ganglion.

test.q: The pterygopalatine ganglion drives secretion from the ___ gland, which makes tears.
test.explain: Postganglionic fibers reach the lacrimal gland through the zygomatic branch of V2 and the lacrimal nerve.

test.q: Which is the largest cervical sympathetic ganglion, sitting near C2-C3?
test.explain: The superior cervical ganglion sends fibers along the carotid arteries to the head.

test.q: Fibers from which cranial nerve reach the otic ganglion via the lesser petrosal nerve? (give name or number)
test.explain: The inferior salivatory nucleus sends fibers through CN IX, the tympanic plexus and the lesser petrosal nerve.

kidTest.q: What does the "rest" team of nerves help you do?
kidTest.explain: The rest team helps you relax, digest food and make tears and spit.

kidTest.q: What does the nerve chain in your neck look like?
kidTest.explain: It is a chain of little nerve knots, like beads on a string.

kidTest.q: What happens to messages at a relay station?
choices: They change to a new nerve
kidTest.explain: Like a bus changing drivers, the message passes to a new nerve and travels on.

kidTest.q: What does the "rush" team do to your pupils?
kidTest.explain: Getting ready to run, the rush team makes pupils big.

kidTest.q: The small relay stations of nerves are called g _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: A ganglion is a cluster of nerve cells where messages are passed on.

advancedTest.q: A Horner pupil fails to dilate with hydroxyamphetamine. The lesion is most likely:
choices: In the spinal cord at C8
advancedTest.explain: Hydroxyamphetamine releases stored noradrenaline from intact third-order terminals. Failure to dilate means a postganglionic lesion, such as one from carotid dissection.

advancedTest.q: Why does an Adie tonic pupil show light-near dissociation?
choices: Accommodative fibers outnumber pupillary fibers in regrowth
The midbrain pretectal nucleus is damaged first
The optic nerve conducts light signals too slowly
Sympathetic fibers take over the sphincter muscle
advancedTest.explain: Accommodative fibers outnumber pupillary ones about 30:1. Reinnervating fibers are mostly near-response fibers, so the near reaction is preserved.

advancedTest.q: Frey syndrome after parotidectomy is best explained by:
choices: Facial nerve motor fibers reaching the skin muscles
Chorda tympani taste fibers entering the parotid bed
Sympathetic adrenergic fibers sprouting into the gland
Otic secretomotor fibers reinnervating cholinergic sweat glands
advancedTest.explain: Facial sweat glands are cholinergic, so misdirected parasympathetic auriculotemporal fibers can drive sweating during meals.

advancedTest.q: Why does a third-order Horner lesion usually spare most facial sweating?
choices: The stellate ganglion supplies facial sweat
Sweating is controlled by the facial nerve
Facial sweat glands use noradrenaline release
Sudomotor fibers follow the external carotid
advancedTest.explain: Most facial sudomotor fibers leave with the external carotid plexus, below an internal carotid lesion. Only a medial forehead strip is lost.
